title: What someone said
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Arabic does not backshift. qāla innahu marīḍ is "he said he is ill", and the verb stays exactly where the speaker left it. English pulls its tense back a step — he said he WAS ill — and Arabic has nothing to pull. This is the module's delta and it is one fewer thing to do, not one more.

Pulling the tense back does not sound old-fashioned in Arabic; it changes the meaning. qāla innahu kāna marīḍ says he was ill at some earlier time and is presumably not now. So the English habit does not merely mark you out — it reports something the speaker never said. Report the words in the shape they were said in.

inna is anna's sentence-initial twin, and after qāla it is inna that turns up: qāla inna al-ʿamal ṣaʿb. Everything L3-M3 said about anna is true of it — a noun or an attached pronoun behind it, never a bare verb — and the accusative it imposes is exactly why innahu, innahā and innahum have to attach.

The reporting verbs are vocabulary, not grammar: L2-M10's qāla and its present yaqūl, akhbaranī ("he told me") and saʾalanī ("he asked me"). Who you told is a li- pronoun after qāla — qāla lī, aqūl lahu — and is already built into akhbaranī and saʾalanī.

A yes/no question is reported with hal or mā idhā and NEVER with anna: saʾalanī hal ʿindī waqt, saʾalatnī mā idhā kuntu taʿbān. English says "if" or "whether" here, and a learner who reaches for "that" instead reports a statement rather than a question.

A wh-question keeps its own question word and needs nothing else: saʾalanī mādhā ashtarī. mādhā is L1-M9's limādhā with the li- taken off — "what" against "for what" — and the word order behind it does not move.

sentences.cue: He said work is hard today

words.note: anna's twin, and the one that follows qāla: qāla inna al-ʿamal ṣaʿb. It holds a noun or an attached pronoun exactly as anna does, never a bare verb.

sentences.trap: English says "he said work WAS hard" and pulls the tense back one step. Nothing moves in Arabic: the clause is reported in the shape the speaker used.
sentences.sound: QAA-la IN-na al-ʿA-mal — the n of inna is held doubled, the same held n as anna's, and the two words run together.

variations.cue: He said the restaurant is excellent
variations.changed: what was reported, with the frame untouched

variations.cue: She said the exam is hard
variations.changed: who spoke: qāla becomes L2-M10's qālat

mistake.display: qāla inna al-ʿamal kāna ṣaʿb al-yawm
mistake.script: قال إن العمل كان صعب اليوم
mistake.why: This is English's backshift imported whole. In Arabic it is not a style, it is a claim: kāna says the work was hard at some past moment and no longer is.

sentences.usage: The plain report, and the sentence the rest of the module varies. inna rather than anna is what marks it as somebody else's words.
sentences.mnemonic: Report the words, not the tense you would use.

words.note: inna with the pronoun welded on, for the same accusative reason as L3-M3's annahā: innahu (he), innahā (she), innahum (they). inna huwa does not exist.
"Ill" — marīḍ of a man, marīḍa of a woman. The heavy ḍ at the end is the one in min faḍlika, and the long ī before it carries the stress.

sentences.trap: Three English words — that he is — are one Arabic word here, and none of them is "is". innahu is the particle and the subject together, and the sentence behind it stays verbless.
sentences.sound: IN-na-hu ma-REEḌ — the doubled n then a light -hu, and marīḍ ends heavy and low in the mouth.

variations.cue: She said she is ill
variations.changed: both halves turn feminine: qālat, innahā, marīḍa

variations.cue: He said he is busy today
variations.changed: what was reported about him

mistake.why: English's "he said he was ill" copied across. In Arabic that reports a different thing — that he had been ill earlier — so the plain report is qāla innahu marīḍ.

sentences.usage: The shortest report there is, and the one a learner will hear most: somebody passing on why another person is absent.
sentences.mnemonic: innahu carries the he; nothing else has to.

sentences.display: akhbaranī anna hind dhahabat ilā al-jāmiʿa
sentences.script: أخبرني أن هند ذهبت إلى الجامعة
sentences.cue: He told me that Hind went to the university
sentences.literal: He-told-me that Hind went(f) to the-university

words.note: "He told me" — the -nī on the end is the me, so no separate word is needed. akhbaratnī is she told me, and khabar ("a piece of news") is the same root.

sentences.trap: English needs a word for "me" and Arabic does not: it is the -nī welded onto the verb. Adding lī after akhbaranī says the me twice.
sentences.sound: akh-BA-ra-nee — the throaty kh right after the opening a, and the -nī at the end is long and unstressed.

variations.cue: She told me that the bill is expensive
variations.changed: who spoke: akhbaranī becomes akhbaratnī

variations.cue: He told me that Hind is ill today
variations.changed: a verbless clause reported instead of a past one

mistake.why: English's "he told me" has two words and this keeps both. The -nī already is the me: akhbaranī anna hind dhahabat, with nothing after the verb.

sentences.usage: How a piece of news is passed on. akhbaranī is warmer than qāla lī and is what you use for something you were told directly.
sentences.mnemonic: akhbaranī has the me inside it.

sentences.cue: He asked me whether I have time today

words.note: "He asked me", with the same -nī as akhbaranī. The hamza in the middle is written and heard: saʾala, a catch between the two a's.
"Time" as an amount of it, which is what ʿindī holds: ʿindī waqt, "I have time". For a clock time the word is still L2-M6's as-sāʿa.

sentences.trap: English can report this with "if" — he asked me if I had time — and "if" in Arabic is idhā, which would make it a condition. A reported yes/no question takes hal or mā idhā and nothing else.
sentences.sound: sa-ʾA-la-nee hal ʿIN-dee — the catch after the first sa is what separates saʾala from a word with none.

variations.cue: He asked me whether I have time tomorrow
variations.changed: when: today becomes tomorrow, and nothing else moves

variations.cue: Hind asked whether I am busy
variations.changed: who asked, and the question behind hal turns verbless

mistake.why: anna reports a STATEMENT. Put it here and the sentence says he told you that you have time, rather than asking: saʾalanī hal ʿindī waqt.

sentences.usage: The commonest reported question of all, and hal is what keeps it a question rather than a claim.
sentences.mnemonic: hal asked it; hal reports it.

sentences.cue: She asked me whether I was busy

words.note: "Whether" — two words learned as one, and hal's slightly more formal twin in a reported question. The idhā inside it is not L3-M4's "if" and opens no condition.

sentences.trap: The idhā sitting inside mā idhā is the same spelling as the conditional "if", and it is doing a different job. The phrase is learned whole, which is why nothing here takes a past for the future.
sentences.sound: maa i-DHAA — two long vowels in a row with a light catch between them; the phrase is said as one unit.

variations.cue: He asked me whether I was tired
variations.changed: who asked, and what was asked about

variations.cue: She asked me whether I am busy
variations.changed: mā idhā swapped for hal, which reports the same question

mistake.why: English's "if" pulls a learner to the conditional idhā on its own. Alone it means "if" and builds a condition; the reported question needs the whole phrase — mā idhā.

sentences.usage: The written and slightly more careful of the two, where hal is the everyday one. Both are correct here.
sentences.mnemonic: mā idhā is whether; idhā alone is if.

sentences.cue: He asked me what I buy from the market

words.note: "What" — L1-M9's limādhā with the li- taken off: "for what" against "what". It stands at the front of its clause and needs no hal beside it.

sentences.trap: Nothing turns around here. English inverts a direct question — what do I buy — and straightens it again when reporting; Arabic never inverted it in the first place.
sentences.sound: MAA-dhaa — a long a, the soft dh of hādhā, and a long a again; limādhā is the same word with two syllables in front.

variations.cue: She asked me what I buy
variations.changed: who asked, and the market dropped

variations.cue: He asked me when I go to work
variations.changed: the question word: mādhā becomes L1-M4's matā

mistake.why: hal reports a yes/no question and this one is not: it asks WHAT. The question keeps its own word — saʾalanī mādhā ashtarī min as-sūq.

sentences.usage: A reported wh-question, which needs no machinery at all beyond the word that was already in the question.
sentences.mnemonic: mādhā asks what; limādhā asks for what.

sentences.cue: He says the restaurant is excellent

words.note: The present of L2-M10's qāla, on L1-M4's prefix law: ya- for he, ta- for you or for she. Its long ū is what lam would cut short.

sentences.trap: A present reporting verb changes nothing behind it. yaqūl inna and qāla inna hold the same clause in the same shape, because the clause never moved for the past one either.
sentences.sound: ya-QOOL IN-na — the long ū is held, and it is the vowel that would vanish behind lam: lam yaqul.

variations.cue: She says the restaurant is expensive
variations.changed: the person, still the prefix: ya- becomes ta-

variations.cue: He says he is always busy
variations.changed: the noun after inna becomes an attached pronoun

mistake.why: After a verb of saying the twin used is inna, not anna. anna is what aʿtaqid and akhbaranī take: yaqūl inna al-maṭʿam mumtāz.

sentences.usage: What somebody says as a habit rather than on one occasion — a standing opinion of theirs.
sentences.mnemonic: qāla is what he said; yaqūl is what he says.

sentences.display: qāla lī inna al-ḥisāb ghālī jiddan
sentences.script: قال لي إن الحساب غالي جدًا
sentences.cue: He told me the bill is very expensive
sentences.literal: He-said to-me that the-bill expensive very

words.note: L1-M9's li- with M1's -ī on it: "to me". qāla lī is "he said to me", and lahu is "to him". akhbaranī needs none of this — the me is already inside it.

sentences.trap: English's "he told me" has the person as a bare object; Arabic's qāla reaches it through li-. Say qāla-nī and there is no such verb; the person needs the preposition.
sentences.sound: QAA-la lee — lī is one light syllable that leans on the verb before it, not on the clause after.

variations.display: qāla lī inna hind dhahabat ilā al-jāmiʿa
variations.script: قال لي إن هند ذهبت إلى الجامعة
variations.cue: He told me that Hind went to the university
variations.changed: the clause reported, now with a past verb behind inna

variations.cue: She told me the bill is cheap
variations.changed: who spoke and what they said about the bill

mistake.why: This attaches the me straight to qāla the way akhbaranī does. qāla does not take it: the person is reached with li- — qāla lī.

sentences.usage: The neutral "he told me", and the difference from akhbaranī is one of warmth rather than of grammar.
sentences.mnemonic: qāla needs lī; akhbara already has it.

sentences.display: qālat innahā lam tanam, hādhā khabar sayyiʾ
sentences.script: قالت إنها لم تنم، هذا خبر سيئ
sentences.cue: She said she didn't sleep — that's bad news
sentences.literal: She-said that-she not she-sleep, this news bad

words.note: "News" — countable in Arabic where English's is not, so khabar sayyiʾ is one piece of bad news. It is the root inside akhbaranī, which is literally "he newsed me".

sentences.trap: A past inside a report stays past and does not go back a further step. English has "she said she hadn't slept" for this and Arabic has only the one past: lam tanam, exactly as she said it.
sentences.sound: KHA-bar — two short syllables opening on the throaty kh, and the -bar does not lengthen.

variations.cue: He said he didn't sleep yesterday
variations.changed: who slept, with L3-M4's yanam behind lam

variations.cue: That's good news, thank you
variations.changed: the judgement flips, using L3-M3's jayyid

mistake.why: This is English's "she hadn't slept" built out of two Arabic pasts. lam tanam is already the past denial, and kānat in front of it belongs to nothing.

sentences.usage: A report with a judgement attached, which is L3-M3's opinion frame running underneath somebody else's words.
sentences.mnemonic: One khabar is one piece of news.

sentences.display: aqūl lahu inna hādhā khaṭaʾ kabīr
sentences.script: أقول له إن هذا خطأ كبير
sentences.cue: I tell him this is a big mistake
sentences.literal: I-say to-him that this mistake big

words.note: L2-M10's qultu in the present, on L1-M4's a- prefix: "I say". naqūl is we say. The long ū is the same one yaqūl holds.

sentences.trap: English chooses between "say" and "tell" by whether a person follows. Arabic uses one verb and adds the person with li-: aqūl is both, and lahu is what makes it "tell him".
sentences.sound: a-QOOL la-hu — the long ū carries the stress and the -hu after it is light and quick.

variations.cue: I tell him this is right
variations.changed: the judgement reported, using L3-M3's ṣaḥīḥ

variations.cue: We say the exam is hard
variations.changed: the person: I becomes we, and the listener is dropped

mistake.display: aqūl lahu anna hādhā khaṭaʾ kabīr
mistake.script: أقول له أن هذا خطأ كبير
mistake.why: anna is what a verb of thinking takes. A verb of saying takes its twin: aqūl lahu inna hādhā khaṭaʾ kabīr.

sentences.usage: Reporting your own words back, which is how a disagreement is described after it has happened.
sentences.mnemonic: One verb for say and tell; li- makes the difference.

comprehensionPool.cue: He said he is busy today
He told me the restaurant is excellent
He asked me whether I have time tomorrow
She asked me whether I was tired
He asked me what I buy from the market
He says the exam is hard

comprehensionPool.script: قال لي إن هند ذهبت إلى الجامعة
comprehensionPool.cue: He told me Hind went to the university
I tell him this is necessary
